people.title: People
people.subtitle: who use the app
people.signIn: Sign in with Microsoft Entra ID

ghost.title: No outside data yet
ghost.body: Bring in a Fabric warehouse, SQL database, lakehouse or semantic model, or call Azure services from functions.

signs.user: Delegated: runs as whoever is signed in, with their own Fabric access.
signs.app: Application: runs as {{who}}, the same for everyone.
signs.key: A key or token the function sends itself, not a Fabric sign-in.

who.owner: the owner of the Fabric app

inspector.grantFabric: A role on its Fabric workspace, or permission on the item.
inspector.opensEverywhere: At its own address and inside Fabric

people.lead: People open the app at its address or inside Fabric and sign in with their work account. To let someone in, select Share in the app bar.

app.lead: Rayfin runs the app as one Fabric app item: its pages, sign-in, database and functions, set up from rayfin/rayfin.yml.

identity.keyLead: These calls don’t use a Fabric sign-in. The function sends its own key or token (or none, for a public API), so anyone who holds that key has the same access, whoever is using the app.
identity.noSecrets: None. Add keys in Code → Secrets and read them from ctx.Secrets, so they never sit in the code.
identity.userLead: These connections are delegated: every query runs as the person using the app, through an on-behalf-of token exchange. Fabric checks their own permissions, so each person only sees what they’re allowed to.
identity.everyoneNeeds: Everyone who uses the app needs access to
identity.userNote: Give people, or a group they’re in, a role on each workspace or permission on each item. Without it they get an authorization error.
identity.appLeadVia: These connections use application access: one shared identity, the owner of the Fabric app item. Everyone sees the same data there, and per-person rules can’t tell people apart.
identity.appLead: Connections that use the app identity have application access: one shared identity, the owner of the Fabric app item. Everyone sees the same data there, and per-person rules can’t tell people apart.
identity.whoServicePrincipal: Service principal that publishes the app
identity.whoAccount: Your Fabric account, which publishes this app
identity.whoOwner: Owner of the Fabric app item
identity.previews: Previews run as {{who}}, which deploys them from pull requests.
identity.ownerNote: The owner is the account that created the app by publishing it first. If someone else published it first, it runs as them.
identity.localNote: When the app runs on your computer, functions use your own sign-in instead, so a call that works there can still fail once the app is published.

website.lead: The app’s pages: the HTML, JavaScript and CSS built from its code, served from the Fabric app.
website.publicNote: Anyone with the link can download the page files, but not the app’s data: that still needs sign-in, and entity rules decide what each person sees. That’s usual for web apps. To load the pages only after a Fabric sign-in, set assetAccess: protected.
website.protectedNote: The page files only load for people signed in to Fabric.

signin.lead: People sign in with their Microsoft Entra ID work account. The app gets a session that says who they are.

database.lead: The app’s own tables, in its Fabric SQL database. Reads and writes use the user’s identity, and each table’s rules decide which rows they can see and change.

storage.lead: Blob storage for files people upload. It’s experimental and not available in every Fabric region.

functions.lead: Server-side code. Calls to outside services use the app identity; reading the app’s own data still uses the identity of the user who called the function.

connectors.lead: Existing Fabric data the app reads and writes through Rayfin connectors. Each one uses the user’s identity or the app identity, set by auth.type in rayfin/rayfin.yml.

secrets.lead: API keys, passwords and connection strings for the functions. Their values stay out of the code: the published app keeps its own, and so does your computer when the app runs there. rayfin.yml keeps only their names and descriptions, and functions read them as ctx.Secrets.NAME.
secrets.noValue_one: The published app has no value for {{names}}, so a function that reads it fails there.
secrets.noValue_other: The published app has no value for {{names}}, so a function that reads them fails there.

status.loading: Checking which values the published app has…
status.notDeployed: Values for the published app can be added once it’s published.
status.team: Shows the published app’s values. The published app and each person’s preview keep their own.
status.updateRayfin: Update the app’s Rayfin version to see which values are set.
status.errorSignIn: Couldn’t check the published app’s values. Your Fabric sign-in may have expired.
status.error: Couldn’t check the published app’s values.
status.ready: Values are write-only: Fabricator shows whether one is set, never what it is.

secrets.localNote: When the app runs on your computer, its functions read local values instead of the published app’s.

source.apiLead: A web API the functions call. Rayfin doesn’t sign these calls in: the code sends its own key or token.
source.suggested: Rayfin can reach {{title}} with the app identity through AudienceType.{{audience}}, so the functions don’t need a key for it.
source.alwaysUser: {{kind}} connectors always use the user’s identity.
source.sameRows: Everyone sees the same rows, so per-person rules on its tables can’t tell people apart.
source.ownAccess: Each person’s own Fabric access applies, and per-person rules on its tables can use who they are.
